title: PACELC and latency trade-offs
description: Learn the PACELC theorem which extends CAP to include latency considerations. Understand how to balance consistency, availability, latency, and partition tolerance.

data.text: The PACELC theorem extends the CAP theorem by adding latency as a consideration. It states: **if there is a Partition (P), you trade off between Availability (A) and Consistency (C); Else (E), when the system is running normally, you trade off between Latency (L) and Consistency (C).**
CAP only tells you what happens during a network partition. PACELC adds that even when there's no partition, you still face a trade-off between consistency and latency.
This is the same as CAP—you must choose between Availability and Consistency.

items: Choose Availability (PA): System stays up, may return stale data
Choose Consistency (PC): System may reject requests to avoid inconsistency

data.text: When there's no partition, you trade off between Latency and Consistency.

items: Choose Latency (EL): Fast responses, eventual consistency
Choose Consistency (EC): Slower responses, strong consistency

data.title: Key Insight
data.text: Strong consistency requires coordination, which adds latency. If you need low latency, you must accept weaker consistency guarantees.

items.title: PA/EC (Partition-Available / Else-Consistent)
items.description: Available during partitions, consistent otherwise. Example: DynamoDB with eventual consistency by default but can be configured for strong consistency during normal operation.

items.title: PC/EC (Partition-Consistent / Else-Consistent)
items.description: Consistent in all cases. Highest latency always. Example: Traditional relational databases with synchronous replication.

items.title: PA/EL (Partition-Available / Else-Latent)
items.description: Always available, always fast, always eventual. Lowest latency. Example: Cassandra with write-level consistency ONE.

items.title: PC/EL (Partition-Consistent / Else-Latent)
items.description: Rare combination—consistency during partitions but latency optimization otherwise. Example: Systems that use quorum writes but cache reads aggressively.

data.text: Latency directly impacts user experience and system throughput. Understanding the latency-consistency trade-off helps you make better architectural decisions.

items: Strong consistency requires synchronous replication across nodes
Synchronous replication adds network round-trip time to every operation
Eventual consistency allows local operations to complete immediately
Caching reduces latency but risks stale data

data.text: Use PACELC to reason about your system's design choices.

items: Social media feeds: PA/EL—availability and latency matter more than perfect consistency
Financial transactions: PC/EC—consistency is non-negotiable, latency is acceptable
Shopping carts: PA/EC—availability during outages, consistency when healthy
Analytics: PA/EL—fast writes, eventual aggregation is acceptable

data.title: Design Tip
data.text: Many databases offer tunable consistency levels. You can choose per-operation: strong consistency for critical writes, eventual for reads. This gives you flexibility within a single system.
